label: thm:ftc1
title: First Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
statement: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[\min(a,b), \max(a,b)]$, and let $x \in (\min(a,b), \max(a,b))$. Then the function $F(u) = \int_a^u f(t)\,dt$ has derivative $f(x)$ at $x$. In Mathlib this is \texttt{intervalIntegral.integral\_hasDerivAt\_right}.
proof: Since $f$ is continuous on $[\min(a,b), \max(a,b)]$ and $x$ is in the interior, $f$ is interval integrable on $[a, x]$ (by Lemma~\ref{lem:continuous_integrable}) and strongly measurable at $x$. By uniform continuity of $f$ on the compact interval (Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform_continuity}), for any $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $|f(t) - f(x)| < \varepsilon$ for $|t - x| < \delta$. Using the integral norm bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_bound}), the difference quotient error satisfies $\left\|\frac{1}{h}\int_x^{x+h} (f(t) - f(x))\,dt\right\| \le \varepsilon$ for $|h| < \delta$, giving $F'(x) = f(x)$.
